title: CrowdStrike Buys Zscaler: Cut Costs or Chase Cross-Sell?
topic: Sequencing cost savings and cross-selling after a $43.9 billion security software merger
hook: CrowdStrike will pay $43.9 billion in stock for Zscaler and promises $500 million in savings and $1 billion in new revenue. Which promise comes first?
tension: Cutting overlapping costs quickly delivers the $500 million target the company controls most, but the cuts can hit the same teams that must win $1 billion of cross-selling to 8,000 new customers.
disclosure: Educational case built from public company releases as of November 27, 2026. It is not investment advice, and the ratios in Exhibit 2 are our arithmetic, not figures the companies report.
brief: On November 23, 2026, CrowdStrike agreed to buy Zscaler. CrowdStrike sells endpoint security on its Falcon platform: software that protects laptops, servers and cloud workloads. Zscaler runs a cloud network that checks traffic between users and applications under a "zero trust" model, where no user or device is trusted by default. The all-stock deal values Zscaler at about $43.9 billion. Zscaler shareholders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares per share, an implied $260.41, about 34% above Zscaler's November 20, 2026 closing price.

The buyer is growing fast. In the quarter ended October 31, 2026, CrowdStrike's annual recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly value of subscriptions in force) grew 27% to $6.26 billion, including a record $419.2 million of net new ARR. Zscaler reported $3.9 billion of ARR for its latest fiscal quarter. CrowdStrike guided fiscal 2027 non-GAAP income from operations, a profit measure that leaves out stock pay and some other costs, of $1,540.9 million to $1,544.3 million. Its non-GAAP subscription gross margin was 82%.

CrowdStrike made two promises. Costs: $500 million a year of savings within 18 to 24 months after closing. Revenue: about $1 billion a year of extra revenue by the end of that period, building over the first 30 months. The company says about 8,000 Zscaler customers do not yet buy from CrowdStrike, and the two already share more than 2,000 customers and 16 product integrations.

CrowdStrike has not said where the savings will come from or how cross-selling will be organised. Both targets lean on the same people: the sales teams who know the customers and the engineers who connect the products. Zscaler's founder will keep running the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike's board. The deal needs Zscaler shareholder and regulatory approval and is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal 2028.

question.text: You lead integration planning at CrowdStrike for the two years after closing. When the cost target and the cross-selling target compete for the same people and budget, decide which one your plan protects first, and defend the call with the numbers.

parts.label: Read the numbers
parts.prompt: What do the ratios in Exhibit 2 say about how much each promise matters to the deal, and which one is harder to hit?

parts.label: Your call
parts.prompt: Choose which target your plan protects first. Say where savings should come from, what you would leave untouched in the first year, and why.

parts.label: Who loses
parts.prompt: Who pays for your choice (employees, customers or shareholders), and how would you limit the damage?

parts.label: When to switch
parts.prompt: What result, measured when, would make you change priorities?

rubric.name: Reading the data
rubric.measures: Whether the answer sizes both promises against the right base and judges which one is riskier.
rubric.excellent: Compares the revenue target with Zscaler ARR and with record net new ARR, turns revenue into gross profit before comparing it with the cost target, and explains why revenue synergies depend on customers while cost synergies depend mostly on management.
rubric.weak: Says $1 billion is bigger than $500 million and stops, or treats revenue and savings as the same kind of money.

rubric.name: A clear, sequenced decision
rubric.measures: Whether one target is protected first and the plan says concretely where savings come from and what is ring-fenced.
rubric.excellent: Commits to one priority, names which kinds of cost to take first and which teams to protect in year one, and links the choice to the numbers and to the price paid.
rubric.weak: Says to do both equally, or picks one with no link to where the money comes from.

rubric.name: Who loses and how to limit it
rubric.measures: Whether the answer names the real losers of its own plan and a credible way to reduce the harm.
rubric.excellent: Names a specific group that loses (for example duplicate back-office staff, or shareholders waiting longer for margin, or Zscaler customers who use rival endpoint tools) and gives one concrete mitigation.
rubric.weak: Claims nobody loses, or lists everyone without a mitigation.

rubric.name: A measurable trigger
rubric.measures: Whether the answer sets a dated, numeric test that would change the plan.
rubric.excellent: Gives a metric, a threshold and a date, such as revenue synergy run-rate against a straight-line path a year after closing.
rubric.weak: Says the team will monitor progress, with no number or date.

rubric.name: Use of numbers throughout
rubric.measures: Whether figures from the case support each claim across all parts, used accurately and without invented data.
rubric.excellent: Uses at least three case figures correctly, labels ratios as estimates, and does not invent churn, overlap or headcount numbers the companies have not disclosed.
rubric.weak: Uses no numbers, misreads a ratio, or invents a statistic.

model_answer.summary: Protect cross-selling first. Take savings from back office, duplicate infrastructure and tools, and ring-fence customer-facing sales and integration engineering for the first year. Switch to a cost-first plan if revenue synergies fall well behind a straight-line path.

parts.text: The revenue promise is worth more but is harder. At CrowdStrike's 82% margin, $1 billion of revenue is roughly $820 million of gross profit, above the $500 million of savings. But it equals 25.6% of Zscaler's ARR and 2.4x CrowdStrike's best-ever quarter of net new ARR, and it depends on customers choosing to buy. Savings are mostly in management's control and already equal 32.4% of fiscal 2027 operating income guidance. At 11.3x Zscaler's ARR, the price only works if growth continues.

Protect revenue. Zscaler is 38.4% of the combined $10.16 billion of ARR, so disrupting it is costly. Take savings first from duplicate offices, back-office systems, cloud infrastructure and overlapping marketing. Ring-fence account teams for the 8,000 Zscaler-only customers and the engineers behind the 16 integrations for the first year. Cut sales overlap only after accounts are mapped. Savings will arrive later than 24 months in this plan, but a lost customer costs both ARR and the cross-sell.

Back-office staff lose first, and shareholders wait longer for the full margin benefit. Zscaler customers who use rival endpoint tools may fear being pushed to switch. Limit it with clear, early severance and retention pay for key staff, and a public commitment that Zscaler keeps working with other endpoint products for a set period.

A straight line to $1 billion over 30 months implies about $400 million of run-rate a year after closing. If cross-sell run-rate is well below that at the one-year review, or gross retention of Zscaler customers drops, accelerate the remaining cost cuts.

alternatives.option: Cost first: hit $500 million fast, then cross-sell
alternatives.better_when: CrowdStrike's own growth slows or its share price falls, so the all-stock price needs visible margin proof early, and customer overlap turns out larger than the release suggests.

alternatives.option: Run Zscaler as a separate unit for a year, with no cuts
alternatives.better_when: Early signs show Zscaler customers leaving over lock-in fears, so keeping the brand and partners stable matters more than either synergy.

alternatives.option: Bundle-led: one combined price for Falcon plus Zscaler from day one
alternatives.better_when: Shared customers already buy both and a bundle can speed cross-selling without new sales staff.

common_traps.trap: Comparing $1 billion of revenue with $500 million of savings directly
common_traps.why: Revenue carries costs; savings drop straight to profit. Turn revenue into gross profit first (about $820 million at an 82% margin) and remember that revenue depends on customers saying yes.
The question is about running the integration, not whether the price was fair or whether to buy either stock.

common_traps.trap: Promising both targets in full and on time
common_traps.why: The case is about what gives when they collide for the same people. A plan with no priority and no trigger skips the trade-off.

common_traps.trap: Inventing overlap, churn or headcount figures
common_traps.why: Neither company has disclosed where savings come from or how many staff overlap. Use the disclosed figures and say what you would need to learn.
